strengths: The core idea—augmenting CVaR-PG with a quantile (VaR) term that admits dynamic programming and thus uses all sampled trajectories—is intuitive, well-motivated (CVaR = expectation of VaR over the tail), and clearly addresses the well-documented 'blindness to success' and gradient-vanishing issues of standard CVaR-PG.

The theoretical development is fairly rigorous: a new soft-quantile VaR Bellman operator is proposed with a proven contraction property (Prop 3.1) and convergence to the true optimal quantile value (Prop 3.2), and the paper carefully establishes how a Markovian policy's induced quantile value function can still be used to execute the (generally history-dependent) optimal VaR policy via cumulative-reward tracking (Props 3.3–3.4), which is a nontrivial and interesting extension of Hau et al. (2025) to the Markovian policy class.

The extension of the VaR Bellman equation to random (rather than deterministic) per-step rewards is a useful, clearly derived technical contribution (Appendix A.2) that broadens applicability beyond the original Hau et al. framework.

Empirical evaluation spans three qualitatively different domains (discrete maze, discrete-action LunarLander, continuous-action InvertedPendulum) specifically designed so that risk-averse behavior is objectively verifiable (not just via return), and results are averaged over 10 seeds with standard errors reported, plus multiple relevant metrics (return, risk-averse rate, CVaR of return) are tracked rather than return alone.

Comparisons include a reasonably comprehensive and recent set of baselines (CVaR-PG, PCVaR-PG, RET-CAP, MIX, REINFORCE), and the paper is transparent about implementation choices (e.g., avoiding importance-sampling clipping confounds, though noting the MIX exception), with extensive hyperparameter and architecture details in the appendix supporting reproducibility.

The paper is honest about limitations, explicitly noting that convergence of the proposed Markovian VaR-PG update from arbitrary initialization is not proven and remains open, and exploration/domain-selection limitations (e.g., excluding Ant/HalfCheetah due to ill-defined risk-averse behavior) are transparently discussed.
weaknesses: The central practical algorithm (Sec 3.2–3.3, Algo 4) is not proven to converge to any meaningful fixed point; Proposition 3.4 only characterizes the objective at the (unknown) optimal value function v^{π̄*}, and the paper explicitly admits that iterating from arbitrary π̄ and v may not converge to π̄*. This leaves the actual deployed method resting on empirical validation only, undermining the soundness claims built up through the Bellman-operator theory.

The trade-off parameter ω between CVaR-PG and VaR-PG appears to require domain-specific scheduling (fixed 0.5 in Maze, linear decay after 40% of training in LunarLander, decay after 25% in Pendulum) with no principled guidance for setting it, raising concerns about sensitivity and practical tunability that are not analyzed via ablation.

Empirical evaluation is limited to only three relatively small/simple domains (discrete maze, LunarLander, single-joint InvertedPendulum), and the authors themselves exclude more complex MuJoCo environments (Ant, HalfCheetah) citing difficulty in defining risk-averse behavior—this narrows the scope of the significance claims and leaves open how well the method scales to higher-dimensional or more complex risk-averse control tasks.

No ablation isolating the individual contribution of the VaR-PG component versus the multi-step advantage estimation trick (Eq. 14, GAE-style) is provided; since multi-step advantage estimation is also applied to baselines (RET-CAP, PCVaR-PG) per Appendix C, it is somewhat controlled for, but a direct ablation of ω itself (e.g., ω=0 vs ω=1 vs the schedule) would strengthen the causal claim that the VaR augmentation specifically drives the sample-efficiency gains.

The value network monotonicity constraint (base value plus non-negative softplus deltas) and the discretization of quantile levels (I quantiles) introduce approximation error relative to the theoretical continuous-α formulation, but no sensitivity analysis on I or discussion of how discretization error interacts with the contraction/convergence guarantees (which assume continuous α, ϵ=0, κ=0) is provided.

Statistical significance of the reported improvements (e.g., in Figures 2 and 3) is only visually conveyed via shaded standard-error bands; no formal significance testing or effect-size reporting is included despite the use of 10 seeds, which would strengthen claims that CVaR-VaR 'consistently outperforms' other methods.

strengths: The paper builds on a reasonable and intuitive idea: since CVaR is the expectation of VaR over the tail, augmenting CVaR-PG with a VaR-based term that admits a dynamic-programming/Bellman decomposition could help address the well-documented sample-inefficiency and 'blindness to success' issues of trajectory-level CVaR-PG.

Non-trivial theoretical derivations are provided, including a new state-only VaR Bellman operator (Prop. 3.1-3.2) and a demonstration (Prop. 3.3-3.4) that a Markovian-policy VaR-optimal action-value function can recover the VaR-optimal history-dependent policy via cumulative-reward tracking, extending ideas from Hau et al. (2025).

The empirical study is designed around three domains in which risk-averse behavior is unambiguous and verifiable (a hidden high-variance 'trap' state/region), which is a sensible evaluation design choice relative to simply reporting aggregate return.

The method is compared against a reasonably comprehensive set of recent baselines (CVaR-PG, PCVaR-PG, RET-CAP, MIX, REINFORCE) under a consistent on-policy, no-importance-sampling protocol, and shows qualitative improvements (faster convergence, higher risk-averse-action rate, higher CVaR of return) in all three tested domains.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee (Prop. 3.4) only characterizes the fixed point of the proposed Markovian VaR update rule, i.e., it shows the optimal policy satisfies the objective, but the paper explicitly admits that convergence from an arbitrary initialization is unknown. Since the actual algorithm used in the experiments is this unproven iterative procedure (not the fixed point), the soundness of the core empirical contribution rests entirely on empirical observation rather than established theory.

The combined objective in Eq. 7 (CVaR plus a weighted expected-VaR term, trade-off ω) is only equivalent to CVaR at the optimum/when ω→0; for any finite ω actually used in training, the learned policy does not provably optimize CVaR, yet the paper asserts 'this does not alter the CVaR objective' without rigorously bounding the bias introduced by finite ω. The ω-decay schedules differ inconsistently across domains (decayed to 0 in LunarLander/Pendulum, kept fixed at 0.5 throughout in Maze), suggesting ω is an ad hoc, per-domain-tuned hyperparameter rather than a principled component of the method, which undermines the main theoretical justification for the approach.

Experimental validation is narrow: only three relatively small/simple environments are used, and the authors explicitly exclude other MuJoCo domains (Ant, HalfCheetah) used in prior work (Luo et al. 2024) with a weak justification ('risk-averse objectives are ill-defined there'), raising concerns about cherry-picking domains favorable to the proposed method and about generalization to higher-dimensional or more realistic risk-sensitive tasks.

Several baselines (RET-CAP, PCVaR-PG) require a known or tuned ground-truth optimal quantile value q*_α, which is selected via a small discrete grid search per domain; it is unclear whether this grid search was performed with equal care/budget for the proposed method's own hyperparameters (ω, N_QUANTILE, schedules), making the comparison's fairness difficult to assess.

No ablation studies are provided for key design choices (effect of number of quantiles I, sensitivity to ω and its schedule, multi-step λ, the monotonicity-enforcing reparameterization of v), nor is there any computational cost/wall-clock comparison despite the method requiring an additional quantile-value network, multi-step quantile regression, and per-step α tracking, which adds non-trivial overhead relative to simpler baselines.

Results are reported only as mean ± standard error curves over 10 seeds with no formal statistical significance testing, and conclusions about which method 'does not consistently converge' (e.g., RET-CAP in Maze) are drawn qualitatively from plots rather than quantified failure rates.

The paper is dense and notation-heavy, leaning heavily on results and notation from Hau et al. (2025); while this is appropriate for a derivative contribution, the incremental nature of Propositions 3.1-3.2 (essentially porting the action-value Bellman operator to a state-value version) is not clearly distinguished from genuinely new contributions, making the originality and magnitude of the theoretical contribution harder to judge.

No code or implementation release is mentioned, and given the many per-domain hyperparameter choices (learning rates selected from grids, differing ω schedules, specific q*_α choices), reproducibility by an independent party seems challenging without released code.

strengths: The core idea—augmenting CVaR-PG with an expected VaR (quantile) term that admits a dynamic-programming decomposition—is well motivated and intuitive, since CVaR is the expectation of VaR over the tail; this directly targets the well-documented sample-inefficiency and 'blindness to success' issues of CVaR-PG.

The paper provides a solid theoretical foundation: a new VaR Bellman optimality operator is proven to be a contraction (Prop 3.1) with the optimal quantile value as its unique fixed point (Prop 3.2), and the authors carefully extend prior deterministic-reward VaR Bellman results (Hau et al. 2025) to the random-reward case (Appendix A.2), which is a non-trivial and useful technical contribution.

The paper addresses an important practical gap: reducing the history-dependent VaR-optimal policy execution procedure to something usable within the Markovian policy class, with a formal justification (Prop 3.3 and 3.4) that a Markovian policy's own quantile value function suffices to recover its optimal action via cumulative-reward tracking.

Empirical evaluation spans three qualitatively different domains (discrete maze, LunarLander, continuous-control InvertedPendulum) specifically designed so that risk-averse behavior is objectively verifiable (not just return magnitude), which is a stronger evaluation methodology than return-only comparisons common in this literature.

Comparison against a reasonably comprehensive and recent set of baselines (CVaR-PG, PCVaR-PG, RET-CAP, MIX, REINFORCE), with an attempt at fair comparison (removing off-policy IS confounds, matching trajectory batch sizes) and reporting results over 10 seeds with standard errors.

Good transparency in reporting practical implementation details (monotonic quantile network parameterization, multi-step advantage/quantile-regression estimation, hyperparameter search ranges) and including an extensive appendix with full algorithm pseudocode and proofs, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The combined objective in Eq. 7 (ω·CVaR + (1-ω)·E[VaR]) is a heuristic surrogate objective rather than being equivalent to the original CVaR objective in Eq. 1 for ω<1; the paper claims 'this does not alter the CVaR objective' in the abstract, which is only true at ω=1, creating a tension between the claimed preservation of the CVaR objective and the actual algorithm, which relies on ω<1 (or a decaying schedule) in practice for its benefits.

The paper explicitly acknowledges that convergence of the proposed Markovian VaR-PG update (Eq. 11-14) from an arbitrary initialization is an open question (Sec 3.2, Conclusion); combined with the heuristic trade-off parameter ω schedule tuned per-domain (fixed at 0.5 in Maze, decayed in LunarLander/Pendulum), the overall algorithm lacks convergence guarantees, limiting the theoretical rigor claimed for the Markovian reduction relative to the tabular/stochastic-policy case.

Empirical validation is limited to three relatively small/simple domains (a tabular maze, LunarLander, single-joint InvertedPendulum), and the authors explicitly exclude harder MuJoCo domains (Ant, HalfCheetah) citing difficulty defining 'risk-averse' ground truth there—while understandable, this restricts the evidence for scalability and generality of the method to higher-dimensional or more complex control settings.

Hyperparameters such as ω and its decay schedule, the quantile discretization granularity (fixed at 10 quantiles), and κ/ϵ for the soft quantile loss appear to be tuned per domain via informal search rather than through a principled selection procedure, raising concerns about sensitivity and practical tunability of the method in new settings.

The comparison baselines (RET-CAP, PCVaR-PG, MIX) are run with modified settings (no off-policy IS for RET-CAP, smaller batch sizes than original papers) explicitly acknowledged to produce results differing from original papers; while done for fairness, this could also inadvertently disadvantage some baselines relative to their best reported performance, and no ablation isolates how much the proposed method's gain stems from the VaR augmentation itself versus other implementation improvements (e.g., multi-step advantage estimation, monotonic quantile network) that were also added to some baselines but perhaps not optimally tuned.

No formal regret, sample complexity, or convergence rate analysis is provided to quantitatively substantiate the central 'sample efficiency' claim beyond qualitative learning curves; the improvement is demonstrated only empirically via faster/more stable convergence in plots, without statistical significance testing or quantitative sample-efficiency metrics (e.g., episodes-to-threshold).
